hookLine: The police scanned his home—from the street.

captions.text: It is a winter night in 1992,
a little after three in the morning.
A federal agent is parked
on a public street,
looking at an ordinary house across
the road.
He never knocks on the door.
He never steps onto the lawn.
He just raises a device
to his eyes, points
it at the home,
and reads the heat coming off
the walls.
From that heat, he decides he knows
what is happening inside.
No warrant.
No foot on the property. Just a machine, a wall,
and a guess about a stranger's private
life.
Nine years later, the Supreme Court had to answer one question about that quiet moment:
was it a search?
We treat the home as the one place the government cannot reach without a warrant.
Your walls are supposed to be the edge of your private world.
But technology has a way of slipping
around old rules.
A thermal camera does not break down
your door or pick your lock.
It just measures the warmth your house
gives off, and turns that warmth
into a picture of what you might
be doing behind the walls.
Over the next twelve minutes: the freezing night that started it,
the hidden operation the heat gave away,
and the line the Court finally drew
at the front door of every home in America.
The house sat on Rhododendron Drive
in Florence, Oregon —
part of a small triplex,
three homes joined under one roof.
A man named Danny Kyllo lived
in one of them.
Federal agents had come to suspect that he was growing marijuana inside, under lights.
Growing marijuana indoors takes light —
a great deal of it.
Indoor growers run high-intensity lamps
for hours at a time,
and those lamps throw off serious heat
And heat is hard to hide.
It seeps through walls and roofs
and leaks out into the cold night
air, whether you want
it to or not.
So on January 16,
1992, a little after three
in the morning, an agent named William
Elliott sat in a car across
the street with a thermal imaging device
an Agema Thermovision 210.
A thermal imager does not see through walls.
It sees heat.
Almost every object gives off infrared radiation
that human eyes cannot detect,
and the device turns that invisible warmth
into a picture —
black for cool, white for hot,
gray for everything in between.
The scan took only a few minutes, and the picture told a story.
The roof over the garage and one
side wall of Kyllo's home glowed far
hotter than the rest of the house,
and hotter than the neighboring units under the same roof.
To Elliott, that pattern meant one thing: powerful grow lamps, running inside.
He never went in.
He never crossed the yard.
He read the outside of the house, in the dark, and drew a firm
conclusion about the inside.
That conclusion did real work.
Along with a tip from an informant
and unusually high electric bills,
the thermal scan helped Elliott convince
a judge to sign a search warrant
When agents finally went inside,
they found what they expected:
an indoor growing operation with more
than a hundred marijuana plants.
Kyllo was charged with manufacturing marijuana.
He asked the court to throw the evidence out, arguing that the thermal
scan itself was an illegal search
of his home.
When that failed, he pleaded guilty —
but kept the right to appeal
the one question that mattered.
And it was a genuinely hard question.
Think about what the agent actually did.
He stood on a public street,
where anyone is allowed to be.
He aimed a device at the outside of a house.
He measured heat that was already leaking out into the open air.
He never touched the home,
never entered it, never even set foot
on the property.
By the old rules,
that looked like no search at all.
For most of its history,
the Fourth Amendment was about physical trespass
an officer breaking in, going through your drawers,
carrying your things away.
Elliott did none of that.
He simply gathered heat that the house was giving off on its own.
But push a little harder,
and it starts to feel very different.
The entire point of the scan
was to learn what was happening inside
a private home —
something the agent could not see
with his own eyes from the street.
He used a machine to pull private
facts out of the one place
the Constitution guards most closely.
If the government can do that freely,
then the wall around your home is only as private as the next new sensor allows.
So which is it?
A harmless reading of heat in the open air —
or a search of your home by another name?
On June 11, 2001,
the Supreme Court gave its answer,
and it was close —
five justices to four.
The majority opinion came from Justice Antonin
Scalia, and the lineup behind it did
not follow the usual conservative-liberal script;
justices who rarely agreed stood
on the same side.
This was not ordinary politics.
It was a fight about the meaning of the home.
Scalia began with first principles.
"At the very core" of the Fourth
Amendment, he wrote, "stands the right
of a man to retreat
into his own home and there
be free from unreasonable governmental intrusion."
The home is not just another place
the police might search.
It is the place.
And the Fourth Amendment,
the Court said, draws a firm line
at its entrance —
a line that must be "not only
firm but also bright."
Then came the rule that made the case famous.
Where the government uses a device
that is not in general public use
to explore details of a home
that it could not have learned without
physically going inside, that is a search
And a search of a home, without a warrant, is presumptively unreasonable
Notice how carefully that is built.
It does not turn on whether
the officer trespassed.
It turns on the technology reaching past
the wall to reveal the inside.
Scalia's worry looked forward, not back.
If the rule depended only on how
good today's device happened to be,
then privacy in the home would shrink
a little every time a better machine came along.
So the Court fixed the line
at the wall itself:
what the inside of your home holds
is presumptively yours, and pulling it out
with a special device is a search
whether that device reads heat,
or something no one has invented
yet.
Four justices disagreed, and their argument
was not foolish.
Justice John Paul Stevens wrote the dissent
The agent, he said,
never went through the wall. He only measured heat that had already
radiated off the outside surface
of the house and drifted
into the public air.
That, Stevens argued, was "off-the-wall" observation,
not "through-the-wall" surveillance —
closer to smelling an odor that floats
out of a kitchen than to peering
inside a room.
Heat that leaves your house,
in his view, is already out
in the world, and collecting it should
not count as searching your home.
It is a real distinction.
But the majority would not rest the privacy of the home on it.
Whatever you call the heat,
the purpose and the result were the same:
the government learned what was going on inside a house without a warrant.
And that, five justices held,
is exactly what the Fourth Amendment
is there to stop.
It is worth being precise about what
the Court did, and what it did
not do.
It did not ban thermal imaging.
It did not erase the evidence against
Kyllo for good.
It sent the case back down
with a narrower instruction:
this kind of scan is a search,
so it needs a warrant —
and the lower court now had
to decide whether the warrant still stood
up once you set the thermal evidence
aside.
The lesson was not "you can never do this." It was "get a warrant
first."
That difference is the whole point.
The Constitution rarely tells the police
they can never learn something.
Usually it just says:
go to a judge,
show your reasons, and get permission before
you reach into a private space.
Kyllo pulled the home firmly back inside that rule.
And the reason the case still matters lies in the phrase Scalia chose:
technology "not in general public use."
In 1992, the fight was over
a heat camera the size
of a lunchbox.
But the logic reaches much further.
Every year, the tools for sensing what
happens inside a home get cheaper,
smaller, and sharper —
drones overhead, better cameras,
devices that read signals through walls.
Kyllo is the case courts keep returning
to when they ask how far
the government can push those tools before
it needs a warrant.
The strength of the ruling, and its weakness, is that same phrase.
"Not in general public use"
is a moving line.
A device that is exotic today can
sit in everyone's pocket tomorrow —
and the more ordinary a technology becomes,
the weaker your claim that using
it invades your privacy.
The Court protected the home against
the future, but it tied that protection
to a standard the future keeps rewriting
So go back to that agent
in the car, on the freezing street,
a little after three in the morning.
He never knocked.
He never crossed the lawn.
He simply read the heat coming off a stranger's walls and decided he knew
what was inside.
The Supreme Court looked at that quiet, no-contact search —
a search with no break-in
and no trespass at all —
and said the home draws a bright
line, and the government had stepped over
it.
But notice what saved the home here:
walls.
Something solid for the heat to leak
through, an edge the Court could point
to and call the entrance.
The Fourth Amendment grew up protecting exactly
that —
houses, walls, doors, the ground you stand
on.
So what happens when the thing the government wants to reach has no walls around it at all?
When your private words travel as sound
through the open air, or as a signal down a wire
into a glass phone booth on a public sidewalk, where anyone can see you,
but no one is supposed
to be listening?
Long before the heat camera,
the Court faced that exact question,
about a man, a booth,
and a hidden microphone.
The answer moved the Fourth Amendment from protecting places to protecting people.
That is next time.

lines: Tip + power bills + thermal scan → warrant
As private as the next sensor allows
Device 'not in general public use' + reveals the inside = SEARCH
The line sits at the wall
